'''Ascott House''', sometimes referred to as simply '''Ascott''', is a [[Grade II* listed building]]<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1291467|desc=Ascott House |grade=II*|access-date=21 May 2014}}</ref> in the [[Hamlet (place)|hamlet]] of [[Ascott, Buckinghamshire|Ascott]] near [[Wing, Buckinghamshire|Wing]] in [[Buckinghamshire]], England. It is set in a 32-acre / 13 hectare estate. 
Ascott House was originally a farm house, built in the reign of [[James I of England|James I]] and known as "Ascott Hall". In 1873 it was acquired by Baron [[Mayer Amschel de Rothschild]] (of the neighbouring [[Mentmore Towers]] estate). The [[Rothschild banking family of England|Rothschild family]] had begun to acquire vast tracts of land in Buckinghamshire earlier in the century, on which they built a series of large mansions from 1852 onwards. Baron Mayer gave the house at Ascott to his nephew [[Leopold de Rothschild]], who transformed it over the following decades into the substantial yet informal [[English country house|country house]] that it is today.

== Architecture ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=June 2022}}
[[File:Ascott House from its grounds - geograph.org.uk - 6198814.jpg|thumb|left|The garden front. From 1874 until the 1930s the house was almost constantly being extended.]]
[[Leopold de Rothschild]], whose principal country residence was [[Gunnersbury Park]], used Ascott at first as a hunting box, but realising the limitations imposed by its modest size, in 1874 he employed the architect [[George Devey]] to enlarge it.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Our History {{!}} Our Stories {{!}} Ascott House and Gardens |url=https://ascottestate.co.uk/explore/history |access-date=2026-02-25 |website=Ascott Estate |language=en}}</ref> The present half-timbered house is largely the result of that commission. Devey attempted to design a house that rambled as though it had grown and developed over centuries. The project became a lifetime work for Devey as the house was continually expanded during the remainder of the 19th century. The rambling and climbing shrubs he had planted as part of the design of the façades that [[Mary Gladstone]] described in her memoirs are no longer there.

The style of architecture, which could be described as "English cottage meets [[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor]] [[Cheshire]] Manor house" is informal, the ground floor being of red brick, while the floors above are half-timbered.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Unknown Error |url=https://static.nationaltrust.org.uk/waf/waf.html?_event_transid=3354573438 |access-date=2026-02-25 |website=static.nationaltrust.org.uk}}</ref> This rustic design no doubt deliberately reflected the house's original intention as a rural retreat and hunting lodge purely for relaxation and pleasure, and contrasted with the family's alternative country home, the more classical and thus impressive Gunnersbury Park. Other Rothschild houses in Buckinghamshire were all designed in the more formal styles of architecture, either the classical renaissance such as Mentmore or that of a French [[château]] as at [[Waddesdon Manor]]. The architecture at Ascott was not intended to faithfully reproduce that of an earlier era. Devey was a forerunner of the [[Arts and Crafts movement]] and had developed a rustic style of his own. Huge bay windows provide views over the [[Chiltern Hills]]. Multiple gables of varying heights with roof lines sweeping to different levels resemble those later designed by the more notable [[Edwin Lutyens]].

== Interior ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=June 2022}}
[[File:Letter (1).jpg|thumb|right|200px|"Lady receiving a letter" by [[Ludolph de Jongh]] (1616–1679), bought by Baron Lionel de Rothschild in 1842]]
On the death of Mrs. Leopold de Rothschild in 1937 the house was inherited by her son [[Anthony Gustav de Rothschild]]. He and his wife, the former Yvonne D'Anvers, enlarged the house further, and were responsible for the present interiors, full of notable paintings and (unusually for a Rothschild house) a large collection of 18th-century English furniture.

The ground floor contains the principal suite of large reception rooms, and while these rooms are furnished with works of art and furniture, they are low ceilinged, and, continuing the informal concept of the design, are in no way intended to be [[state room]]s. The entrance hall is notable for its large paintings by [[Thomas Gainsborough]], [[George Romney (painter)|George Romney]], and [[Joshua Reynolds]] and the large work by [[George Stubbs]], ''Five Mares''. The dining room, now decorated with what appear to be Dutch tiles but is in fact ''[[trompe-l'œil]]'', contains a collection of small, mainly Dutch, paintings from the 16th and 17th centuries by such artists as [[Aelbert Cuyp]], [[Adriaen van Ostade]] and [[Jan Steen]].

The works of art continue through the common room, with its portrait of a prelate attributed to [[Lorenzo Lotto]]. The Drawing Room today displays a collection of [[Blue and white pottery|blue Chinese ceramics]] with examples from the [[Han dynasty]] {{Circa|206 BC}}, to the [[Qing dynasty]] which lasted from 1644 until 1911. This room contains the painting of the ''Madonna and Child with St. John'' by [[Andrea del Sarto]] of 1520.

In 1936 the Billiards Room was transformed into a library to house the many volumes amassed by Anthony de Rothschild. One of the most comfortable rooms in the house, its book-lined walls are only interrupted by Gainsborough's full-length portrait of the Duchess of Richmond, and various other masterpieces. Standing on a console table is [[Giovanni Battista Tiepolo|Tiepolo]]'s "The Assumption of the Virgin". The room also contains furniture by [[Thomas Chippendale]] and ancient [[Chinese ceramics]].

== Gardens ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=June 2022}}
[[File:Ascott House - The Madeira Walk.jpg|thumb|200px|The "Madeira Walk", a path between two mirror [[herbaceous border]]s, terminated by [[George Devey]]'s classical [[pavilion]]]]
[[File:Ascott House - Venus Fountain.jpg|thumb|200px|The [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]] fountain by [[Thomas Waldo Story]]]]
The extensive manicured gardens were laid out on the advice of the garden designer Sir [[Harry Veitch]] {{circa|1902}} by Leopold de Rothschild as a wedding present to his wife. A sundial made entirely of topiary complete with Latin numerals proclaims in clipped yew: "Light and shade by turn, but love always".

Closest to the south front of the house are paved areas of gardens in the style of [[Gertrude Jekyll]], and from these across large areas of lawn are the terraced gardens. The dominating feature of these individual gardens is the clipped hedges, [[topiary]] and flowering shrubs. The largest feature of the garden is the [[bronze]] fountain representing ''[[Venus (mythology)|Venus]] in her shell [[chariot]] attended by [[cherub]]s'', by the American sculptor [[Thomas Waldo Story]]. Story was also responsible for the fountain in the Dutch flower garden. This garden, so named for its displays of tulips in spring, is approached by descending a flight of steps through a [[rock garden]], complete with dripping [[grotto]] and artificial [[stalagmite]]s. In the centre of the garden Story's tall fountain, crowned by [[Cupid]] supported by dolphins, is surrounded by a formal bedding scheme.

From the entrance front's adjacent garden of topiarised [[Buxus|box]] and [[Bay laurel|bay trees]] a long-grassed [[Avenue (landscape)|avenue]], enclosed by a tall beech hedge, leads to the [[lily]] pool. This pool, originally created for [[Ice skating|skating]], is the heart of a [[Giverny|Monet-style garden]], complete with a [[thatch]]ed summerhouse also designed by George Devey.

==Cricket ground==
Cricket was first played at Ascott House on 28 August 1880, when an eleven brought from London played an eleven selected by a Mr. Tennant, whose players were partly from London and partly from the area surrounding the estate. Leopold de Rothschild was present for this first match.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ascottestate.co.uk/page9.htm|title=Cricket at Ascott|publisher=www.ascottestate.co.uk|access-date=15 August 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110722132627/http://www.ascottestate.co.uk/page9.htm|archive-date=2011-07-22|url-status=dead}}</ref> The Rothschild family played a prominent role in the formation of [[Buckinghamshire County Cricket Club]]. Buckinghamshire first played at Ascott House in the 1905 [[Minor Counties Championship]] against [[Hertfordshire County Cricket Club|Hertfordshire]], playing there regularly once a season to 1979.<ref name="MCM">{{cite web |url-access=subscription |url=https://cricketarchive.com/Archive/Grounds/11/848_minc.html|title=Minor Counties Championship Matches played on Ascott Park, Wing|publisher=CricketArchive|access-date=15 August 2011}}</ref>

The county returned to Ascott in 1998 to play an [[MCCA Knockout Trophy]] match against [[Berkshire County Cricket Club|Berkshire]]. Minor Counties Championship cricket was last played there in 2003,<ref name="MCM"/> with Buckinghamshire's last venture to the ground coming 2009 in the MCCA Knockout Trophy against [[Lincolnshire County Cricket Club|Lincolnshire]].<ref>{{cite web |url-access=subscription |url=https://cricketarchive.com/Archive/Grounds/11/848_mint.html|title=Minor Counties Trophy Matches played on Ascott Park, Wing|publisher=CricketArchive|access-date=15 August 2011}}</ref> The ground held a [[List A cricket|List A match]] once, which came in the [[2003 Cheltenham & Gloucester Trophy]] when [[first-class cricket|first-class]] county [[Gloucestershire County Cricket Club|Gloucestershire]] were the visitors.<ref>{{cite web |url-access=subscription |url=https://cricketarchive.com/Archive/Grounds/11/848_a.html|title=List A Matches played on Ascott Park, Wing|publisher=CricketArchive|access-date=15 August 2011}}</ref> The match was something of a mismatch, with Gloucestershire scoring a massive 401/7, then bowling Buckinghamshire out for 77 to win the match by 324 runs.<ref>{{cite web |url-access=subscription |url=https://cricketarchive.com/Archive/Scorecards/76/76939.html|title=Buckinghamshire v Gloucestershire, 2003 Cheltenham & Gloucester Trophy|publisher=CricketArchive|access-date=15 August 2011}}</ref>

== Ascott today ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=June 2022}}
[[File:Ascott House - the drive.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The approach to the principal entrance, lined by clipped [[Bay laurel|bay trees]]]]
Ascott House, with some of its important [[art]] collection and a small part of the estate, was given in 1947 to the [[National Trust]] by Anthony de Rothschild. The National Trust market the property under the name "Ascott". However, as at nearby [[Waddesdon Manor]], the Rothschild family retain a very close control. The last resident of the house was the son of the donor, Sir [[Evelyn de Rothschild]], who died in 2022. He added further works of art and ceramics to the collection and much of what is seen in the collection is still privately owned by the Rothschild family.

Sir Evelyn de Rothschild also expanded the estate to its present size of approximately 3200 acres (13 km<sup>2</sup>). The estate contains many miles of new road-side tree planting, well-kept hedging, and cropping and planting of new woodland but retains some of the older permanent pasture and small fields. A major new road, the [[A505]] ploughs through the area between the house and its [[Horse breeding|Stud Farm]], but has been disguised by dense woodland planting.

The house retains very much the feel of a private home, and is open to the public in the afternoon of many weekdays during summer.

'''Claydon House''' is a [[English country house|country house]] in mid-Buckinghamshire, England, near the village of [[Middle Claydon]].{{sfn|Estate Office|2012}} It was built between 1757 and 1771 and is now owned by the [[National Trust]].

The house is a [[Listed building#England and Wales|listed Grade I]] on the [[National Heritage List for England]], and its gardens are listed Grade II on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref name=NHLEHouse>{{NHLE|num=1288461|desc=Claydon House|access-date=26 December 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref><ref name=NHLEGarden>{{NHLE|num=1000597|desc=Claydon|access-date=26 December 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>

==History==
Claydon has been the ancestral home of the [[Verney family]] since 1620.<ref name=knox6>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=6}}.</ref> The church of All Saints, Middle Claydon lies less than {{convert|50|yard}} from the house and contains many memorials to the Verney family: among them Sir [[Edmund Verney (Cavalier)|Edmund Verney]], who was chief standard bearer to [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] during the [[English Civil War]].<ref name=knox6/> Sir Edmund was slain at the [[Battle of Edgehill]] on 23 October 1642,<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Page |editor-first=W.H. |editor-link=William Henry Page |date=1927 |series=[[Victoria County History]] |title=A History of the County of Buckingham, Volume 4 |publisher= |location= |pages=32–35 |url= http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=62527 }}  Parishes : Middle Claydon{{snd}}Manor</ref> defending the standard.<ref name=knox49>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=49}}.</ref> His ghost is reputed to haunt the house.{{sfn|Ash|1973}} In 1661, following the [[English Restoration|Restoration of the Monarchy]], Sir Edmund's son (Sir [[Sir Ralph Verney, 1st Baronet, of Middle Claydon|Ralph Verney]]) was awarded a [[baronetcy]] by [[Charles II of England|Charles II]] for his and his father's loyalty and bravery during the preceding period of unrest. Sir Ralph's second surviving son and heir, John Verney was later, in 1703, made [[Viscount Fermanagh]] and his son was [[Ralph Verney, 1st Earl Verney|Ralph Verney]], in 1743, was created [[Earl Verney]].<ref name=knox49/>

There is believed to have been a house on the site from at least the 1400s. The manor of Middle Claydon was purchased by Sir [[Ralph Verney (MP for City of London)|Ralph Verney]], [[Lord Mayor of London]], in 1463. However, the land was immediately leased to Sir Roger Giffard and the first recording of the house on site describes the Tudor brick H-shaped manor house of the Giffards in 1539. Sir Edmund Verney the Standard Bearer redeemed the leased in 1620 and it became the principal country seat of the Verneys from that point onwards. The house received some modifications in the seventeenth century, particularly in 1654 when Sir Ralph Verney, 1st Bt, returned from his political exile and began to rebuild the family fortune after the Civil War. The house was virtually rebuilt starting in 1757 by [[Ralph Verney, 2nd Earl Verney]].<ref name=knox6/> Later in 1759, Lord Verney constructed a new west wing for the house faced in stone to provide a suite of [[state apartments]]. Following his election as MP for Buckinghamshire in 1768, Verney vastly expanded this house to create a new central [[rotunda (architecture)|rotunda]] entrance hall and ballroom wing.<ref name=knox8>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=8}}.</ref> The original conception was of a mansion to rival the richer [[Stowe House|Earl Temple]]'s huge mansion at [[Stowe, Buckinghamshire|Stowe]], a few miles away near [[Buckingham]].<ref name=knox6/> However, the house as it stands today is a fraction of its original planned size as the ballroom and rotunda were dismantled in 1791-92 after the Earl's death. Lord Verney ran into financial problems before the latter two wings were entirely completed, and had to spend the final years of his life on the continent to escape his creditors.<ref name=knox10>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=10}}.</ref> The estate was inherited by his niece, Mary Verney, 1st Baroness Fermanagh in 1791, who sold off much of the family's land and sold the unfinished wing of the house off brick by brick.<ref name=knox10/>

[[File:All Saints Church, Middle Claydon, Bucks, England - tower from NW.jpg|thumb|right|All Saints' parish church, Middle Claydon, in the grounds of Claydon House]]

==Exterior==
The exterior of the house is quite austere – seven bays in total, on two floors, with a three-bayed central prominent elevation surmounted by a [[pediment]]. The fenestration is of [[sash windows]]. (The ground floor windows are crowned by small round windows suggesting a non-existent mezzanine.) The centre bay contains a large central venetian window on the ground floor.<ref name=knox12>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=12}}.</ref>

==Interior==
By contrast to the exterior the interiors are an extravaganza of [[rococo]] architecture in its highest form. The principal rooms: the north hall, a double cube room ({{convert|50|x|25|x|25|ft|m|abbr=on|adj=mid| high}}) may have lost its adjoining hall under the lost dome. However, its magnificence remains. The broken pedimented door cases are adorned with rococo carving, by [[Luke Lightfoot]], the most talented wood carver of the era, who worked extensively on the great mansion.<ref name=knox13>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=13}}.</ref> His work can be found on the ceiling and the niches in the walls. The adjoining saloon is slightly more restrained in its decoration. However the ornate carving continues into the dado rails, and onto the Corinthian columns supporting the huge [[Venetian window]].<ref name=knox15>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=15}}.</ref> The third principal room was redecorated as a library by Parthenope, Lady Verney in 1860. The plaster rococo ceiling remains in all its splendour.<ref name=knox19>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=19}}.</ref>

A staircase of inlaid [[ivory]] and [[marquetry]] leads to the first floor. The walls of the staircase hall are ornamented with medallions and carved garlands reflecting the theme established in the main reception rooms. The wrought iron balustrade of the stairs contains ironwork ears of wheat, which rustle like the real thing as one ascends the flights.<ref name=knox21>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=21}}.</ref>

The marvel of the first floor is the Chinese room: one of the most extraordinary rooms in the house if not England. Here the rococo continues, but this time in a form known as [[chinoiserie]] — essentially a Chinese version of the rococo decorative style. The entire room is a fantasy of carved pagodas, Chinese fretwork, bells and temples while oriental scrolls and swirls swoop around the walls and doors reaching a crescendo in the temple-like canopy, which would have once contained a bed, but now gives a throne-like importance to a divan.<ref name=knox31>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=31}}.</ref>

Also on this floor is a small museum dedicated to the [[nursing]] pioneer [[Florence Nightingale]], the sister of Parthenope, Lady Verney. In her later years Nightingale regularly stayed at the house.<ref name=knox28>{{harvnb|Knox|1999|p=28}}.</ref>

==Claydon House today==
The present [[Verney baronets#Verney baronets, of Claydon House (1818)|Verney family]], are the descendants of [[Sir Harry Verney, 2nd Baronet|Sir Harry Calvert, 2nd Baronet]] who inherited the house in 1827. He was very tenuously related to the Verneys only through marriage. However, he adopted the name Verney on inheriting. The house was given to the National Trust in 1956 by [[Sir Ralph Verney, 5th Baronet]].<ref name=knox47>{{harvp|Knox|1999|p=47}}.</ref> His son, [[Sir Edmund Verney, 6th Baronet]], a former [[High Sheriff of Buckinghamshire]], lived in the house until 2019.{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}

Annually (usually the last weekend in July) at Claydon House, there is a [[hovercraft]] race meeting organised by the Chilterns Branch as part of the [[Hovercraft Club of Great Britain]] (UK) National Hovercraft Racing Series.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.hovercraft.org.uk/ |title=HCGB Chilterns Branch Hovercraft Race}}, UK.{{verification needed|date=April 2015}}</ref>

===As a film and TV location===
{{Uncited section|date=October 2025}}
Claydon House has appeared in a number of films. Interiors were used for [[Emma (1996 theatrical film)|''Emma'']] in 1996. In 2013, Claydon House was used for interior and exterior shots for filming ''[[Far from the Madding Crowd (2015 film)|Far from the Madding Crowd]]'', a British film version of [[Thomas Hardy]]'s novel.<ref>{{cite web |title=Far from the Madding Crowd filmed at Claydon |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/discover/film-tv/far-from-the-madding-crowd-filmed-at-claydon |website=National Trust |access-date=18 February 2026}}</ref> In 2018, the interiors were used for [[The Aeronauts (film)|''The Aeronauts'']], and again in 2020 for [[Cinderella (2021 American film)|''Cinderella'']].{{cn|date=October 2025}} The house also appeared in the third season of [[Bridgerton]] (2024) and [[Downton Abbey: The Grand Finale]] (2025).<ref>{{cite web |last1=Phillips |first1=Jessica |title=How to visit all of the ‘Downton Abbey’ country houses in the UK |url=https://www.timeout.com/uk/news/how-to-visit-all-of-the-downton-abbey-country-houses-in-the-uk-091125 |website=Time Out |access-date=18 February 2026 |date=11 September 2025}}</ref> Claydon House also featured in episode four of [[David Dimbleby]]'s 2010 BBC documentary series "[[Seven Ages of Britain (2010 TV series)|Seven Ages of Britain]]".

[[File:Parque de Ashridge House.jpg|thumb|View from Bridgewater Monument to the house]]
'''Ashridge''' is a [[Estate (land)|country estate]] and [[stately home]] in [[Hertfordshire]], England. It is situated in the [[Chiltern Hills]], an [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]], about {{convert|2|mile|km}} north of [[Berkhamsted]] and {{convert|23|mile|km}} north west of London. The estate comprises {{convert|5000|acre|km2}} of woodlands (known as Ashridge Forest), commons and chalk downland which supports a rich variety of wildlife.

Today, Ashridge is home to [[Hult Ashridge]], [[Hult International Business School]]'s executive education programme, as it has been since 1959. The estate is currently owned by the [[National Trust]].

==History==

===Ashridge Priory===
{{main|Ashridge Priory}}
In mediæval times, Ashridge was the location of [[Ashridge Priory]], a [[College (canon law)|college]] of the monastic order of [[Bonhommes]] founded in 1283 by [[Edmund, 2nd Earl of Cornwall|Edmund, 2<sup>nd</sup> Earl of Cornwall]], whose [[palace]] was at nearby [[Berkhamsted Castle]].<ref>"according to Tanner", from the [https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02672b.htm Boni Homines] article in the [[Catholic Encyclopedia]]</ref> At the [[dissolution of the monasteries]] the priory was surrendered to the crown and King [[Henry VIII]] used it to house his children, namely Prince Edward and the Princesses Mary and Elizabeth.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.greatbritishlife.co.uk/people/unearthing-the-past-in-ashridge-7098310|title=Unearthing the past in Ashridge|date=22 September 2011|website=Great British Life}}</ref> Eventually he bequeathed the property to his daughter [[Elizabeth I of England|Elizabeth]]. The priory church was demolished during the reign of Elizabeth I.<ref>[https://archive.today/20140617093235/http://www.ashridge.org.uk/website/content.nsf/wCOR/History+of+Ashridge?opendocumentHistory of Ashridge – Ashridge Business School], Accessed 17 June 2014</ref>

===The Egerton family===
{{main|Egerton family}}
In 1604, the estate became the property of [[Sir Thomas Egerton]].<ref>Sanecki, K. A. pg 25</ref> Egerton's son, [[John Egerton, 1st Earl of Bridgewater|John Egerton]], was created 1<sup>st</sup> [[Earl of Bridgewater]] on 27 May 1617. In 1800, redevelopment of the estate as the Bridgewater residence was begun by [[Francis Egerton, 3rd Duke of Bridgewater|Francis Egerton, 3<sup>rd</sup> Duke of Bridgewater]]. The Duke demolished most of the Priory and after his death, the present house was constructed between 1808 and 1814 by [[John Egerton, 7th Earl of Bridgewater|John Egerton, 7<sup>th</sup> Earl of Bridgewater]]. The 3<sup>rd</sup> Duke of Bridgewater was buried in the Egerton family vault in [[Little Gaddesden]] Church, close to Ashridge.<ref>[https://www.littlegaddesdenchurch.org.uk/Bridgewater_Chapel.html Bridgewater Chapel at Little Gaddesden Church], accessed 24 July 2015</ref>

In 1848, the estate passed to the [[Baron Brownlow|Earls Brownlow]], another strand of the Egerton family,<ref>Sanecki, K. A. pg 6</ref> and then in 1921 it was split, with the land passing to the National Trust, while the house and garden was acquired by speculators.<ref name=sanecki73>Sanecki, K. A. pg 73</ref>

===Conservative Staff College===

In 1928, [[Urban Hanlon Broughton]] purchased the house as a gift for the [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], intended to commemorate [[Bonar Law]].<ref name=sanecki73/> In July 1929, Ashridge opened by [[Stanley Baldwin]] as a College under the governance of the Bonar Law Memorial Trust (BLMT).<ref>"Bonar Law College", Daily Herald, 2 July 1929 page 7</ref> The BLMT was charged by its Founding Deed to pursue the following goals, namely:

(a) honouring the memory of a great statesman, 

(b) the preservation of the house and grounds as an historic building, 

(c) to create an educational centre ... 

(d) to train lecturers, speakers and writers to further the study of the subjects outlined above 

(e) ... provide lectures and/or discussions on these subjects open to the public or for those who had paid fees to attend, 

(f) ... provide a supporting staff, 

(g) to allow boarding by those attending the lectures and discussions.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Berthezène|first1=Clarisse|title=Ashridge College, 1929-54: a glimpse at a Conservative intellectual project|journal=Contemporary British History|date=Spring 2005|volume=19|pages=79–93|doi=10.1080/1361946042000303873|s2cid=144485487}}</ref>

For the next fifteen years the college, the full title of which was the Bonar Law Memorial College, Ashridge was to act as a school for Conservative intellectuals creating, in their own words, 'Conservative Fabians', and as a 'College of Citizenship' for 'the general education of the electorate'. Associated with the College were regional or county circles or clubs, such the [[Ashridge Dining Club]] in London; their activities were reported by The Ashridge Journal.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=Autumn 1937|title=The London Ashridge 1937 Club|journal=The Ashridge Journal|pages=45–46}}</ref> In 1954, its Deed of Foundation was changed by Act of Parliament, and Ashridge was 're-founded' as an educational charity. In 1959, it became a Management College, which it remains today.<ref>A glimpse at the archives of a Conservative intellectual project</ref>

===Hult International Business School===
{{main|Hult Ashridge|Hult International Business School}}

In 1959, Ashridge College was re-launched to provide management training, and was named [[Hult Ashridge|Ashridge Business School]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://home.btconnect.com/peter-grainger/rhs/ashridgecollege.html|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120305172054/http://home.btconnect.com/peter-grainger/rhs/ashridgecollege.html|url-status=dead|title=Rural Heritage Society|archivedate=5 March 2012}}</ref> In 2015, Ashridge Business School operationally merged with Hult International Business School, an American business school with campuses in seven cities around the world. As part of the merger, ''Ashridge Business School'' changed its name to [[Ashridge Executive Education]], later [[Hult Ashridge]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ashridge.org.uk/about-us/governance/|title=Governance|website=Ashridge.org.uk|access-date=5 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160402171716/https://ashridge.org.uk/about-us/governance/|archive-date=2 April 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Estate==
===Ashridge House===
[[File:Hult Ashridge.png|thumb|Ashridge is a noted example of early  [[Gothic Revival architecture]] and features decorative [[battlement|crenellation]]s]]
[[File:James-Wyatt-1800.webp|thumb|upright|Architect [[James Wyatt]]]]
[[File:Ashridge House - the Chapel - geograph.org.uk - 1568938.jpg|thumb|upright|Ashridge chapel]]
Prior to his death in the early 1800s, the 3<sup>rd</sup> Duke of Bridgewater had begun to demolish the [[Medieval Priory]] buildings in order to build a new country house. His successor, the 7<sup>th</sup> Earl of Bridgewater commissioned the architect [[James Wyatt]] to build his new home, Ashridge House. The [[foundation stone]] for the new house was laid by the 7<sup>th</sup> Earl's wife, [[Charlotte Catherine Anne, Countess of Bridgewater]], on 25 October 1808, the 48<sup>th</sup> anniversary of the accession of [[George III of Great Britain]]. The ceremony is commemorated by a brass plaque by the main entrance.<ref>{{cite book |title=Views of the Seats of Noblemen and Gentlemen, in England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland; [Ser. 1-2] |year=1829 |publisher=Reid |page=5 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Pn133unQAsIC&dq=Charlotte+Catherine+Anne,+Countess+of+Bridgewater&pg=PP47 |language=en}}</ref>

In 1813, part-way through the construction works, Wyatt died unexpectedly, and the building project was completed the following year by his nephew Jeffry Wyatt (later known as Sir [[Jeffry Wyatville]]).<ref>Sanecki, K.A., pg 30</ref> The present house is regarded as one of the finest examples of early [[Gothic Revival architecture]] and is now a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref>[http://www.hha.org.uk/HHA/Property.aspx?id=923&vw=0 Historic Houses Association] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091227064315/http://www.hha.org.uk/HHA/Property.aspx?id=923&vw=0 |date=27 December 2009 }}</ref><ref name=pevsner>Pevsner pp.238–240</ref><ref>{{NHLE |num=1348442 |desc=Grade I |access-date=10 April 2013}}</ref>

Ashridge house was built on the site of the 13<sup>th</sup>-century priory building which had been demolished in 1800. Some parts of the old priory were incorporated into the house by James Wyatt, including the [[undercroft]] of the monastic [[refectory]], featuring two [[aisle]]s, seven [[Bay (architecture)|bay]]s and a [[Vault (architecture)|rib-vaulted]] ceiling, which he repurposed as a beer cellar below the dining room and drawing room.<ref name=englishheritage>{{NHLE|desc=Ashridge Management College |num=1348442 |access-date=13 August 2012 }}</ref>

The mansion is built of [[ashlar]] faced with [[Totternhoe stone]] with a [[castellated]] [[parapet]] and low-pitched [[slate]] roofs. It features a variety of [[casement window]]s including [[pointed arch]] and [[ogee]] lights typical of the early Gothic Revival style. Before his untimely death, James Wyatt completed the north-facing front entrance and the central block, containing the state apartments and western courtyards. Jeffry Wyatt added private apartment blocks at an angle to the main building and an orangery with a turret in 1815–17. The main entrance features a projecting [[porte-cochère]] and octagonal turrets, added by Jeffry Wyatt c.1814.<ref name=englishheritage/>

Inside the mansion are a number of richly decorated [[state room]]s; of the interior features, only the hall, the staircase tower and the chapel are Gothic in design. The high staircase hall features a stone stair with iron railing, surrounded by niches containing statues by Sir [[Richard Westmacott]]. At the centre of the [[fan vaulting|fan-vaulted]] ceiling is a large dial connected to the [[weather vane]] on the roof which displays the current wind direction. The Brownlow Hall contains a giant [[frieze]] of the goddess [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]] surrounded by [[putti]] with an [[armorial]] centrepiece and three early-Twentieth Century murals. Redecoration of the interiors was commissioned by Lady [[Marian Alford]] and executed in the [[neoclassical architecture|neoclassical]] style in 1855–63 by Sir [[Matthew Digby Wyatt]], including a replica of [[Guido Reni]]'s [[:File:Guido Reni - Aurora - WGA19273.jpg|Aurora]] ceiling and [[Aedicule|aedicular door surrounds]]. Among the alterations carried out after the conversion of the mansion into a college, the [[Conservatory (greenhouse)|conservatory]] was altered by [[Clough Williams-Ellis]] in 1919 to form a dining-room. The boundary between [[Hertfordshire]] and [[Buckinghamshire]] originally passed through the dining room, though the house is now entirely in [[Hertfordshire]].<ref name=pevsner/><ref name=englishheritage/>

The house incorporates a Gothic Revival Chapel designed by James Wyatt, completed by Jeffry Wyatt in 1817. The most notable exterior feature of the chapel is its [[spire]] which was demolished in 1922 by Lord Brownlow as it had become structurally unsound. The spire which can be seen today is in fact a [[fibreglass]] replica which was erected in 1969. The chapel interior features a pair of Fourteenth-Century carved doors, fan-vaulted [[coving (interior design)|coving]] supporting a [[cant (architecture)|cant]]ed panelled ceiling; a set of carved [[oak]] [[choir stall]]s designed by Jeffry; and an array of [[Rayonnant]] [[lancet window]]s.<ref name=pevsner/> The windows were originally fitted with [[stained glass]] panels depicting scenes from the Bible; the glass was imported by the 7<sup>th</sup> Earl from Germany, having been originally designed in the Sixteenth Century for [[Steinfeld Abbey]] and [[Mariawald Abbey]]. The glass was auctioned off at [[Sotheby's]] in 1928 and acquired by the [[Victoria and Albert Museum]].<ref name=vanda>{{cite web|title=Stained glass from Mariawald Abbey|url=https://www.vam.ac.uk/content/articles/s/stained-glass-from-mariawald-abbey/|work=Victoria and Albert Museum|access-date=13 August 2012}}</ref> One glass panel featuring the [[Blessed Virgin]] was placed in the nearby Church of Ss Peter and Paul at [[Little Gaddesden]]; another, depicting [[St Peter]] was in Christ Church, Croydon in London. Beneath the chapel is a vaulted medieval wellhouse with a {{convert|224|ft|adj=on}} [[water well|well]].<ref name=englishheritage/>

===Gardens===
Outside the house stands the [[timber-frame]] and brick Fourteenth-Century Monks' Barn in the Monks' Garden. It was remodelled in 1816 by Jeffry Wyatt who added a covered walkway. In 1884 Mathew Digby Wyatt added the red brick Fern House.<ref name=englishheritage/>

The gardens were laid out from 1813 onwards under the direction of [[Charlotte Catherine Anne, Countess of Bridgewater]], wife of the 7<sup>th</sup> Earl. She commissioned the noted landscape gardener [[Humphrey Repton]], and they formed a friendship on his many visits to the estate. Repton presented many ideas in his ''Red Book'' for the estate in 1813, including a rosarie (or ''[[rosarium]]'') and a "Monks' Garden" commemorating Ashridge's monastic heritage with a layout of grave-shaped flower beds. The Countess approved many of his designs, but also had her own ideas for the estate and made alterations to his proposals. Writing in 1824, the chaplain to the Earl of Bridgewater, Rev [[Henry Todd (priest)|Henry Todd]], noted that "the profusion of flowers which abound here, as the walks and conservatories together with the elegance of their arrangement, sufficiently indicates the care and attention bestowed by the Countess of Bridgewater upon her delightful pursuits of the garden."{{sfn|Way|2013}}<ref>{{cite web |title=Spring Newsletter 2018 and Annual Report |url=https://hertsgardenstrust.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/Spring%20Newsletter%20and%20Annual%20Report%202018.pdf |publisher=Hertfordshire Gardens Trust|access-date=13 March 2021 |page=13}}</ref>{{sfn|Williamson|2020|p=199}}<ref>{{cite journal |title=GC & HTJ. |date=1984 |volume=196 |page=13 |publisher=Haymarket Publishing. |language=en}}</ref> The rosarie and the Monks' Garden are still visible at Ashridge today.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Garden |url=https://www.ashridgehouse.org.uk/explore-ashridge-house/garden/ |publisher=Ashridge Hult |access-date=13 March 2021}}</ref>

===Bridgewater Monument===
[[Image:UK Ashridge Bridgewater monument.jpg|thumb|upright|The Bridgewater Monument]]
The Grade II* listed<ref>{{NHLE |num=1078046 |desc=Grade II* |access-date=10 April 2013}}</ref> [[Bridgewater Monument]] ({{gbmapping|SP970131}}) is a tower on the Ashridge estate, built in 1832 in memory of [[Francis Egerton, 3rd Duke of Bridgewater|Francis Egerton, 3<sup>rd</sup> Duke of Bridgewater]] (1736–1803), "the father of inland navigation".<ref>[http://www.visiteastofengland.com/be-inspired/wildlife/thedms.aspx?dms=13&feature=2&venue=0180642 Duke of Bridgewater Monument at Ashridge Estate]{{Dead link|date=June 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Visit East of England</ref>

===Ashridge Commons and Woods===
{{main|Ashridge Commons and Woods}}

'''Ashridge Commons & Woods''' ({{gbmapping|SP975135}}) is a 640.1 hectare (1581.7 acre) [[Biological Site of Special Scientific Interest]]. The site was notified in 1987 under the [[Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981]] and lies on the [[Buckinghamshire]] and [[Hertfordshire]] border and is home to much semi-natural vegetation. As well as this, the site has extensive areas of woodland, grass and plantations.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1000452.pdf |title=Ashridge Commons and Woods |publisher=[[English Nature]] |access-date=24 February 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090320005745/http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1000452.pdf |archive-date=20 March 2009 |df=dmy }}</ref> Ashridge Woods are also well known for their Bluebell woods.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bt-images.net/inspiring-natural-scenery/|title=Ashridge lavender forest|publisher=BT Images|access-date=24 January 2014}}</ref>

===Later developments===
Part of the estate became [[Ashridge Golf Club]] in 1932, and had [[Henry Cotton (golfer)|Henry Cotton]] as its club professional in the late 1930s, including his most successful year 1937.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ashridgegolfclub.ltd.uk/|title=Home :: Ashridge Golf Club|website=www.ashridgegolfclub.ltd.uk}}</ref>

During the [[Second World War]], the building and the lawn in front of it was used as a secondary site for [[Charing Cross Hospital]].<ref name="WW2 People's War">{{Cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/ww2peopleswar/stories/37/a1993737.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070306105603/http://www.bbc.co.uk/ww2peopleswar/stories/37/a1993737.shtml|url-status=dead|archive-date=6 March 2007|title=WW2 People's War}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Parry |first=Louise |date=23 June 2024 |title=Wartime evacuee babies reunite at historic hospital |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cevv9vdnk5vo |website=BBC}}</ref>

The house has housed the [[Ashridge Executive Education]] program, of [[Hult International Business School]], since 1959.<ref name=heritage>{{cite web|title=History and Heritage |url=http://www.ashridgehouse.org.uk/Website/Content.nsf/wCOR/History+and+Heritage?opendocument |archive-url=https://archive.today/20121223213359/http://www.ashridgehouse.org.uk/Website/Content.nsf/wCOR/History+and+Heritage?opendocument |url-status=dead |archive-date=23 December 2012 |work=Ashridge College |access-date=13 August 2012 }}</ref>
==In popular culture==
Ashridge Common has been featured many times in film and television series due to its distinction as an area of natural beauty. Scenes for: ''[[Maleficent (film)|Maleficent]]'', ''[[Plotlands]]'', ''[[Sleepy Hollow (film)|Sleepy Hollow]]'', ''[[Jonathan Creek]]'' and ''[[Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (film)|Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire]]'' were filmed in Ashridge's [[Frithsden Beeches]] wood.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chilternsaonb.org/caring/stwp_site_details.asp?siteID=414 |title=Special trees and woods – Frithsden Beeches |publisher=Chilterns Conservation Board |access-date=16 February 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110613145351/http://www.chilternsaonb.org/caring/stwp_site_details.asp?siteID=414 |archive-date=13 June 2011 |url-status=dead |df=dmy-all }}</ref> Ashridge House, which is now [[Ashridge Business School]], has been featured in films such as ''[[The Dirty Dozen]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0061578/locations|title=The Dirty Dozen (1967) - IMDb|via=www.imdb.com}}</ref> More recently, it has been used as a location for [[The Crown (TV series)|''The Crown'']] and [[Pennyworth (TV series)|''Pennyworth'']] TV series.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lewis |first1=Katy |title=Ashridge House: How the former home of Henry VIII is branching out |work=BBC News |date=28 December 2022 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/uk-england-beds-bucks-herts-63805173 |access-date=29 December 2022}}</ref>

In early 2023, English singer-songwriter Sam Smith released a music video for his song, ''[[I'm Not Here to Make Friends]]'', almost entirely shot in and outside the property.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/1018815-sam-smith-music-video-filming-nearly-gives-tourists-heart-attack|title=Sam Smith music video filming nearly gives tourists 'heart attack'|date=10 December 2022|newspaper=International News|access-date=12 February 2023}}</ref>

681324.title: Dorneywood
681324.extract:
Dorneywood is an 18th-century house near Burnham in southern Buckinghamshire. Originally a Georgian farmhouse, it has Victorian and later additions, and following a fire in 1910, was remodelled in 1919 by Sir Robert Lorimer. It is a Grade II listed building.
It was given to the National Trust by Lord Courtauld-Thomson in 1947 as a grace-and-favour country home for a senior member of the Government, usually a secretary of state or minister of the Crown.  The Dorneywood Trust has the objective of 'maintaining the mansion house and gardens of Dorneywood'.

main.*:
{{Short description|English country house}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2016}}
{{Use British English|date=September 2019}}
[[File:Dorneywood gate.jpg|thumb|right]]
[[File:Dorneywood.jpg|thumb|right]]
[[File:Dorneywood grounds.jpg|thumb|right]]
'''Dorneywood''' is an 18th-century house near [[Burnham, Buckinghamshire|Burnham]] in southern [[Buckinghamshire]].<ref>{{cite book  | last = Pevsner | first = Nikolaus | authorlink = Nikolaus Pevsner |author2=Elizabeth Williamson |author3=Geoffrey K Brandwood | title = Buckinghamshire | orig-date = 1960 | edition = 2nd | year = 1994 | publisher = Penguin Books | page = 211 | location = London | isbn = 0-14-071062-0 }}</ref> Originally a [[Georgian architecture|Georgian]] farmhouse, it has Victorian and later additions, and following a fire in 1910, was remodelled in 1919 by Sir [[Robert Lorimer]].<ref>Dictionary of Scottish Architects: Robert Lorimer</ref> It is a Grade II listed building.<ref>{{NHLE |num=1332660 |desc=Dorneywood |grade=II |access-date=11 January 2025}}</ref>

It was given to the [[National Trust]] by [[Lord Courtauld-Thomson]] in 1947 as a [[grace-and-favour]] country home for a senior member of the [[Her Majesty's Government|Government]], usually a [[Secretary of State (United Kingdom)|secretary of state]] or [[minister of the Crown]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/5035592.stm |title=UK | UK Politics | Dorneywood: A ministerial retreat |publisher=BBC News |date=1 June 2006 |access-date=13 June 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-dorneywoodgarden |title=Visitor information |publisher=National Trust |accessdate=13 June 2013 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110911132355/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-dorneywoodgarden |archivedate=11 September 2011 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>  The Dorneywood Trust has the objective of 'maintaining the mansion house and gardens of Dorneywood'.<ref>[http://www.charitycommission.gov.uk/registeredcharities/ScannedAccounts/Ends66%5C0000213166_ac_20081231_e_c.pdf 2008 Accounts and Annual Report]{{dead link|date=December 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

==Occupancy of the house==
The [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom|prime minister]] alone [[Powers of the prime minister of the United Kingdom#Other powers and constraints|has the right to decide]] which minister or secretary of state is to occupy the house. In previous administrations it has been the residence of the [[chancellor of the exchequer]] and, prior to 31 May 2006, was occupied by [[Deputy Prime Minister of the United Kingdom|Deputy Prime Minister]] [[John Prescott]]. Prescott was forced to relinquish occupancy of Dorneywood, following a series of scandals over an affair with civil servant Tracey Temple and a snatched paparazzi photograph of him playing [[croquet]] on the lawn of the property whilst the Prime Minister [[Tony Blair]] was out of the country on a visit to [[Washington, D.C.|Washington]].<ref name="autogenerated1">{{cite news|url=http://news.sky.com/skynews/Home/Sky-News-Archive/Article/20080641223370?f=rss |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120711231907/http://news.sky.com/skynews/Home/Sky-News-Archive/Article/20080641223370?f=rss |url-status=dead |archive-date=11 July 2012 |title=Prescott Gives Up Dorneywood Home |work=Sky News |date=1 June 2006 |accessdate=13 June 2013 }}</ref> However, given the controversies over John Prescott's use of the house, senior politicians were reluctant to use it.<ref name="autogenerated1"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/politics/article2532776.ece |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100604123312/http://www.timesonline.co.uk/tol/news/politics/article2532776.ece |url-status=dead |archive-date=4 June 2010 |title = The Times & The Sunday Times}}</ref> The house was eventually taken over by [[Alistair Darling]], Chancellor of the Exchequer when [[Gordon Brown]] became prime minister in 2007.<ref>[https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/politics/7734802/Grace-and-favour-homes-for-Osborne-Hague-and-Clegg.html ''Telegraph'', 18 May 2010, "Grace-and-favour-homes"]</ref> "A spokesman for Mr Brown ... explained that the house ... was owned by a trust, and would revert first to the [[Lord Mayor of London]] and then to the [[List of ambassadors of the United Kingdom to the United States|American Ambassador]], if the Chancellor did not want it."<ref>[https://www.independent.co.uk/news/grace-but-should-they-still-be-in-favour-1255614.html ''Independent'', 13 June 1997, "Grace... but should they still be in favour?"]</ref>

Various former prime ministers (before achieving the premiership) have occupied the house, among them [[Anthony Eden]]. On becoming prime minister, [[Alec Douglas-Home]] was reluctant to forsake the more comfortable and modern Dorneywood for the antique splendours of [[Chequers]]. Another, [[James Callaghan]] as [[Foreign Secretary (United Kingdom)|foreign secretary]], also had the use of Dorneywood (later [[Chevening]] was to become the official country home for the holder of that office).

In 2010, [[George Osborne]], the Chancellor of the Exchequer, took occupancy of the house.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/8689187.stm |title=Hague and Clegg given timeshare of official residence |publisher=BBC News |date=18 May 2010 |access-date=13 June 2013}}</ref>  It was also used by Osborne's successors, [[Philip Hammond]], [[Sajid Javid]], [[Rishi Sunak]], [[Jeremy Hunt]] and [[Rachel Reeves]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2016/jul/18/boris-johnson-forced-to-share-mansion-with-liam-fox-and-david-davis|title=Boris Johnson forced to share mansion with Liam Fox and David Davis|last1=Mason|first1=Rowena|last2=Sparrow|first2=Andrew|date=2016-07-18|website=The Guardian|access-date=2016-07-27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dorneywood.org/past-residents|title = Past Residents}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Stacey |first1=Kiran |title=Angela Rayner passed over as Reeves given use of Dorneywood mansion |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2024/sep/17/angela-rayner-passed-over-as-reeves-given-use-of-dorneywood-mansion |website=The Guardian |access-date=10 August 2025 |date=17 September 2024}}</ref>

==Interior==
[[File:Rex Whistler - Ave Silvae Dornii 1928.jpg|thumb|180px|A Rex Whistler mural at Dorneywood]]
The interior of the house contains some decorations by [[Rex Whistler]], as well as paintings and furniture belonging to the [[Government Art Collection]]. There is also furniture belonging to the National Trust.

==Grounds==
The National Trust arranges public tours of the house and gardens during the summer. The estate consists of the house and {{convert|215|acres}}<ref>[http://www.burnhamparish.gov.uk/local_history.htm Burnham Parish Council – Local History] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111001081608/http://www.burnhamparish.gov.uk/local_history.htm |date=1 October 2011 }}</ref> of parkland, woodland and farmland.  The grounds are noted for their [[cottage garden|cottage]] and [[kitchen garden]], as well as their [[herbaceous border]]s and [[rose]] displays.<ref>{{cite web|author=England |url=http://www.british-towns.net/attractions/attraction_selected.asp?GetTLID=2170&page=1 |title=DORNEYWOOD GARDEN in Burnham, England. Page: 1 |publisher=British-towns.net |date=4 June 2013 |accessdate=13 June 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3613 |title=Dorneywood Garden – History, Travel, and accommodation information |publisher=Britainexpress.com |accessdate=13 June 2013}}</ref>  The upkeep of the estate is in part supported by the Dorneywood Thomson Endowment Trust Fund.<ref>{{cite news|last=Stone |first=Ollie |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/politics/5036540.stm |title=UK | UK Politics | What are grace-and-favour homes? |publisher=BBC News |date=1 June 2006 |access-date=13 June 2013}}</ref>

922754.title: Coombe Hill, Buckinghamshire
922754.extract:
Coombe Hill is a hill in The Chilterns, located next to the hamlet of Dunsmore, Buckinghamshire, England, near the small town of Wendover, and overlooking Aylesbury Vale.  It is not to be confused with another Coombe Hill on the flank of Haddington Hill, some two miles (3.2 km) to the north-east. It is part of the Bacombe and Coombe Hills Site of Special Scientific Interest.
The majority of the hill (an area of 106 acres (43 ha)) once formed part of the Chequers Estate but was presented to the National Trust by the British government when they were given the Estate in the 1920s.  The summit of the hill is 852 feet (260 m) above sea level.

'''Coombe Hill''' is a hill in [[Chiltern Hills|The Chilterns]], located next to the hamlet of [[Dunsmore, Buckinghamshire]], [[England]], near the small town of [[Wendover]], and overlooking [[Aylesbury Vale]].  It is not to be confused with another Coombe Hill on the flank of [[Haddington Hill]], some {{convert|2|mi|spell=in}} to the north-east. It is part of the [[Bacombe and Coombe Hills]] [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]].

The majority of the hill (an area of {{convert|106|acre|ha|0}}) once formed part of the [[Chequers]] Estate but was presented to the [[National Trust]] by the [[United Kingdom|British]] [[His Majesty's Government|government]] when they were given the Estate in the 1920s.  The summit of the hill is {{convert|852|ft|m}} above sea level.

==Coombe Hill Monument – Second Boer War ==
For most of human history, war memorials were erected to commemorate great victories; remembering the dead was a secondary concern. Coombe Hill Monument is one of the first and largest examples of a war memorial erected to honour the names of individual men who fell whilst fighting for their country.  The monument is an iconic Buckinghamshire landmark and a Grade II [[Listed building|listed monument]]. At {{convert|260|m|order=flip}} above sea level, it sits on one of the highest and most striking spurs of the Chilterns, commanding a wide view of the Vale of Aylesbury. On a clear day, it can be seen from the [[Berkshire Downs]] and the [[Cotswolds]] to the west.  The view overlooks [[Chequers]], the country home of the Prime Minister.

The monument was erected in 1904, by public subscription, in memory of 148 men from Buckinghamshire who died during the [[Second Boer War]]. Coombe Hill Monument was almost totally destroyed by lightning in 1938 and was rebuilt in the same year. The original bronze plaque and decorations were stolen in 1972 and replaced with a stone plaque and iron flag. The new stone plaque was also inscribed with the additional names of nine men believed to have been missing on the original. The monument was again badly damaged by a lightning strike in the early 1990s and spent several months in repair. It is now equipped with conductors to prevent this from happening again. The monument and a few square metres of surrounding land are owned by Buckinghamshire County Council.

The monument is a Grade II a [[listed building]] designated in 1985.<ref>{{Cite web |title=MONUMENT, Ellesborough - 1125886 {{!}} Historic England |url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1125886 |access-date=2022-06-14 |website=historicengland.org.uk |language=en}}</ref>

==The 2010 restoration==
On 21 October 2010, the monument was rededicated after substantial restoration work.  The work was done by [[Buckinghamshire County Council]] with funds raised by the Coombe Hill Monument Appeal Committee.  The committee consisted of:  
The [[Lord Lieutenant of Buckinghamshire]], [[Sir Henry Aubrey-Fletcher, 8th Baronet|Sir Henry Aubrey Fletcher Bt JP]] (Patron);
Major General Stuart Watson CBE (Chairman);
Mark Bailey, [[Buckinghamshire County Council]] (Project Manager);
Lt Col (Retd) Ingram Murray, Honorary Secretary of the Friends of the [[Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry]];
Patricia Birchley, Elected Member, Chiltern Ridges;   
Johanna Sienkiewicz, local resident, Project Researcher;      
Chris Arnold, [[Ellesborough]] Parish Council; 
Pam Priestley, Elected Member [[Wycombe District Council]]; 
Paul Rogerson, Elected Member, [[Buckinghamshire County Council]]; and
Neil Harris, The [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]

==Triangulation point and plaque==
In front of the monument was a rectangular concrete pillar that was the [[Triangulation station|trig point]] and topped with a metal plaque donated in 1988 that pointed to [[true north]] and to the following distant features: [[The Cotswolds]] ({{convert|53|mi}}), [[Brill, Buckinghamshire|Brill]] Hill ({{convert|13|mi}}13 miles), [[Waddesdon Manor]] ({{convert|10|mi}}), [[Calvert, Buckinghamshire|Calvert]] Chimneys ({{convert|15|mi}}), [[Aylesbury]] Church ({{convert|5|mi}}), [[Mursley]] Water Tower ({{convert|15|mi}}), [[Wingrave]] Church ({{convert|8|mi}}), [[Leighton Buzzard]] ({{convert|12|mi}}), [[Mentmore]] ({{convert|9|mi}}), [[Edlesborough]] Church ({{convert|11|mi}}) and [[Ivinghoe Beacon]] ({{convert|9|mi}}).

The trig point and its [[toposcope]] were heavily damaged, bordering on being totally destroyed, by vandals in early October 2018.<ref>{{cite web |title=Video footage shows aftermath at Coombe Hill after vandals attack structure which has stood there since the 1950s |url=https://www.bucksherald.co.uk/news/video-footage-shows-aftermath-coombe-hill-after-vandals-attack-structure-which-has-stood-there-1950s-246652 |website=Bucks Herald |access-date=30 March 2021}}</ref>

==Flora and fauna==
Coombe Hill has 3 different types of land including acid [[heath]]land, chalk grassland and deciduous woodland. It is home to much interesting [[wildlife]] — including [[red kite]]s, [[yellowhammer]]s and [[common firecrest|firecrests]]. It also holds the habitat to many rare plants such as heather, orchids and the [[Chiltern gentian]]. Due to its rarity the acid moorland is a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] (SSSI).

==Coombe Hill Run==
A {{convert|7|km|adj=on}} running race organised by the Vale of Aylesbury Athletic Club which includes {{convert|190|m}} of climbing up to the monument on Coombe Hill, the Coombe Hill Run is a rare example of a [[fell running|fell race]] in southern Britain. First held in 1973, and now held on the first Sunday in June, it attracts more than 150 runners.

==Origin of name==
The word ''coombe'' is of [[Brythonic languages|Brythonic]] origin and means "[[Cirque|hollow]]".

'''Buckingham Chantry Chapel''' (also known as the '''Old Latin School''') is a 15th-century [[chapel]] and a [[National Trust]] property in [[Buckingham]], [[Buckinghamshire]], [[England]]. The chapel is the oldest building in Buckingham and is noted in particular for its [[Norman architecture|Norman]] doorway. Few buildings in Buckingham date to before the 18th century, as a large fire destroyed much of the town in 1725.<ref name=Long/> The chapel is a [[Grade II* listed]] building, being added to the list by [[English Heritage]] on 13 October 1952.<ref name=EH/>

==History==
The building was originally established as a hospital in the 12th century. It became a [[chantry chapel]] in 1268, founded by Matthew de Stratton, the [[Archdeacon of Buckingham]]. The present building dates from the 15th century, when [[John Ruding]], [[Archdeacon of Lincoln]], undertook rebuilding work in 1471 and 1481.<ref name=Roffey/>

The building was later used by the [[Royal Latin School]], with the chantry priests probably serving as the first schoolmasters. A schoolmaster's house was added to the north.<ref name=Roffey/> The school remained on the site until 1907, when expansion prompted a move to new buildings on Chandos Road.

Further restoration work was undertaken by Sir [[George Gilbert Scott]] in 1875.{{citation needed|date=May 2024}}

The chapel was given to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1912. It is still owned by the Trust, and is open to the public as a second-hand bookshop.<ref name=NT/><ref name=NT2/>

3332929.title: Boarstall Duck Decoy
3332929.extract:
The Boarstall Duck Decoy  is a 17th-century duck decoy located in Boarstall, Buckinghamshire, England, and now a National Trust property. The system took advantage of a two-acre lake with pipe-cage tunnels running out of it.
At one time a common sight in the English countryside, only four duck decoys now remain. The Boarstall Duck Decoy is still in working order, and is surrounded by 13 acres (53,000 m2) of natural woodland.
The intent of the decoy was to catch large numbers of waterfowl.  A decoy or fake duck was used to attract birds onto a small patch of water.  The pond was equipped with a long cone-shaped wickerwork tunnel. A "decoyman" with a trained dog then herded the birds into the tunnel. Once the birds had been trapped in the tunnel, they could then be caught as required.   Originally, the birds trapped here were a source of food. The advantage over simply shooting the birds was that ducks caught by this method did not have pellets or lead shot in their bodies that would have to be removed prior to consumption, allowing them to command higher prices. Today, the National Trust organise demonstrations, and any birds caught are ringed for ornithological study. One duck apparently traveled as far away as Turkey.
